description: Next.js supports two server-side execution runtimes: Node.js (full capabilities, larger startup overhead) and Edge Runtime (v8 isolates, extremely fast startup, restricted APIs). Selecting the appropriate runtime ensures optimal TTFB and allows utilizing specific package ecosystems.

constraints.title: Do Not Use Node.js Built-in Modules in Edge Runtime
constraints.problem: Importing native Node.js APIs (such as fs, path, child_process) inside files configured with export const runtime = 'edge' causes build-time compilation or runtime execution errors.
constraints.whyItMatters: The Edge Runtime utilizes lightweight v8 isolates which exclude the full Node.js standard library. While this yields sub-millisecond cold starts, referencing Node-only modules or dependencies that import them will crash compilation or route routing entirely.
forbiddenPatterns: import fs from 'fs' in routes with export const runtime = 'edge'
import path from 'path' inside files marked as edge runtime target
Referencing process.env.NODE_ENV or native buffer classes unsafely inside edge contexts
allowedPatterns: Using standard browser fetch APIs and Web streams in Edge routes
Defining export const runtime = 'nodejs' when requiring database connectors or filesystem tools
productionRisks: Compilation/build failures when deploying to production hosts
Cold start routing crashes when invoking edge API endpoints
Edge middleware failures blocking all routing pathways
architectureImplications: Necessitates isolating Node-heavy operations to specific Node-only routes
Forces middleware to remain lightweight and restrict package dependencies
optimizationGuidance: Verify all middleware third-party dependencies are edge-compatible before importing them
quickFixes: Change export const runtime = 'edge' to 'nodejs', or replace native Node imports with Web API equivalents (e.g. Web streams)
architectureSuggestions: Establish microservices or isolated Node API endpoints for intensive operations, keeping layouts and edge pages lightweight

invalid: export const runtime = 'edge'; import fs from 'fs'; export async function GET() { const data = fs.readFileSync('file.txt'); return Response.json(data); }
valid: export const runtime = 'nodejs'; import fs from 'fs'; export async function GET() { const data = fs.readFileSync('file.txt'); return Response.json(data.toString()); }

constraints.title: Do Not Execute Raw Database Connection Blocks inside Edge Runtime
constraints.problem: Attempting to instantiate standard ORM database connection pools (like PostgreSQL pg, MySQL mysql2) directly in Edge Routes crashes at build time due to lack of TCP/socket APIs on Edge runtime.
constraints.whyItMatters: The Edge Runtime lacks support for TCP socket connections required by standard SQL databases. If you import a database adapter that connects via raw sockets inside an Edge Route, the application will crash. Database connections on Edge must be made via HTTP/REST database APIs (like Prisma Data Platform, Supabase HTTP, or Neon serverless driver).
forbiddenPatterns: import { Client } from 'pg' inside route files configured with export const runtime = 'edge'
Instantiating new Client() SQL connections globally inside Middleware
allowedPatterns: Using serverless HTTP/WebSocket drivers (like Neon's WebSockets adapter or Prisma Data Proxy) in Edge routes
Configuring data-heavy query routes as export const runtime = 'nodejs'
productionRisks: Uncaught connection exceptions on edge route hit
Deploy failures due to missing module compilation boundaries
Service exhaustion when spawning database drivers globally
architectureImplications: Enforces using modern serverless API endpoints or REST boundaries for dynamic datasets
Pushes database layer configurations to isolated, Node-backed micro-routes
optimizationGuidance: Use Neon serverless websockets or REST-based GraphQL pools when choosing the Edge runtime for fast global delivery
quickFixes: Change the route segment runtime to nodejs or switch database connection initialization to Neon's HTTP or serverless-compatible driver
architectureSuggestions: Create database adapter interfaces that conditionally select between direct TCP in Node runtime and REST-based data proxy APIs in Edge runtime

invalid: export const runtime = 'edge'; import { Client } from 'pg'; export async function GET() { const c = new Client('postgresql://...'); await c.connect(); }
valid: export const runtime = 'nodejs'; import { Client } from 'pg'; export async function GET() { const c = new Client('postgresql://...'); await c.connect(); const res = await c.query('SELECT 1'); return Response.json(res.rows); }

constraints.title: Adhere to the 1MB or 2MB Edge Runtime Code Size Limitation
constraints.problem: Bundling large third-party dependencies into Edge routes or Middleware will cause deployment failures on hosting providers (like Vercel or Cloudflare Workers) due to strict code size caps.
constraints.whyItMatters: The Edge Runtime is built to run on globally distributed lightweight compute boundaries. Major hosting providers enforce a hard code size limit of 1MB (compressed) or 2MB (uncompressed) for edge functions. Exceeding this limit prevents production deployments or leads to instant edge execution failure.
forbiddenPatterns: Importing complete UI components or major visualization suites (e.g. Chart.js, D3) into Edge route handlers
Referencing large natural language processing (NLP) parser models directly inside Middleware
allowedPatterns: Using lightweight REST clients (e.g. native fetch) inside Edge functions to dispatch work to external heavier servers
Restricting Edge route modules to pure coordination logic, authentication validations, and header rewrites
productionRisks: Production deployment rejection by Vercel or Cloudflare CLI pipelines
Unscheduled edge routing outages due to memory overflow
Degraded Cold Start metrics as larger script blocks take longer to initialize
architectureImplications: Forces keeping Edge-based codebases small, modular, and extremely focused
Dictates pushing complex PDF generations, image processing, or heavy parsing workloads to background queues or Node.js endpoints
optimizationGuidance: Analyze bundled middleware output using webpack-bundle-analyzer or visual size analysis tools regularly
quickFixes: Extract large packages from the Edge file and delegate the work via a fetch call to a standard Node.js API route
architectureSuggestions: Adopt a split-execution architecture: use Edge for lightning-fast routing/session verification, but route computationally heavy steps to optimized Node.js backends

invalid: export const runtime = 'edge'; import { heavyPdfGenerator } from 'heavy-pdf-generator'; export async function POST() { return new Response(heavyPdfGenerator()); }
valid: export const runtime = 'nodejs'; import { heavyPdfGenerator } from 'heavy-pdf-generator'; export async function POST() { return new Response(heavyPdfGenerator()); }
